address-circle.title: The address circle must be done in exact order
address-circle.hook: City Hall first. Everything else is locked behind it.
address-circle.body: You cannot open a bank account without a residence card. You cannot get a residence card without registering your address at City Hall within 14 days of arrival. You cannot register your address at City Hall without your passport and visa. The sequence is: land → City Hall → residence card → bank account → everything else. Doing it out of order costs weeks.

three-month-wall.title: Month three is when most people break
three-month-wall.hook: The novelty ends. The loneliness begins. It's survivable.
three-month-wall.body: The first weeks are adrenaline. Everything is new and interesting enough to carry you. Around month three, the adrenaline runs out and reality arrives: you have no close friends yet, your Japanese isn't working the way you hoped, and the city is indifferent. This is normal. Almost everyone goes through it. The people who stay are the ones who knew it was coming.

silence-not-disapproval.title: Silence is not disapproval
silence-not-disapproval.body: In most Western cultures, silence in conversation means something is wrong. In Japan, a long pause before someone answers often means they're taking your question seriously. Rushing to fill silence reads as anxiety and can make the other person feel their thoughtfulness is unwanted. Let it breathe. The answer is coming.

keigo-hierarchy.title: Using casual Japanese to seniors signals you don't respect hierarchy
keigo-hierarchy.hook: Register mistakes aren't just grammar errors. They're social ones.
keigo-hierarchy.body: Japanese has formal registers (keigo) used with bosses, teachers, strangers, and anyone older. Using plain form with a senpai or manager is like calling your professor by their first name on day one — it signals you're claiming equal standing. Nobody will correct you directly. They'll just become slightly more formal and slightly more distant. Learn keigo early, even imperfectly.

eating-alone.title: Eating alone is not sad here. It's infrastructure.
eating-alone.hook: Counter seating exists for a reason.
eating-alone.body: Japan has an entire culture built around solo dining. Ramen shops have counter seats specifically for single diners. Most sushi bars are designed for one. Convenience stores exist so you can eat a full meal standing at 11pm without anyone thinking anything of it. You will never feel judged for eating alone in Japan. It may be the most socially comfortable country in the world for solitude.

konbini-infrastructure.title: The convenience store is not a convenience store
konbini-infrastructure.hook: It's a bank, a pharmacy, a post office, a hot meal, and a social neutral zone.
konbini-infrastructure.body: You can pay your electricity bill at a konbini. You can withdraw cash (7-Eleven ATMs accept foreign cards; most Japanese ATMs don't). You can send packages, print documents, buy medicine, eat a full hot meal, and sit at a table without anyone making you feel like you have to leave. In a city where public sitting space is scarce, the konbini is infrastructure.

line-not-optional.title: LINE is not optional
line-not-optional.hook: If your employer, school, or friends are Japanese, you will use LINE or you will be excluded.
line-not-optional.body: Japan runs on LINE the way the US runs on iMessage and Europe runs on WhatsApp. Work groups, school announcements, event coordination, apartment lease communication — it all happens on LINE. Not having it or checking it slowly means missing things. There's also a timing norm: messages sent in the evening are generally replied to the next morning, not immediately. Read receipts are visible, which creates its own social pressure.

foreigner-network.title: There is a foreigner network. It takes effort to find.
foreigner-network.hook: It exists in every city. It is the difference between surviving and belonging.
foreigner-network.body: Every major Japanese city has overlapping communities of long-term foreign residents — expat Facebook groups, meetup language exchanges, international bars that became community hubs, subreddit threads turned real friendships. These networks feel secondary to 'really living in Japan,' but they are where most people find their footing. Your first Japanese friends will often come after your first foreign-resident friends give you the confidence to try.

sarah-tokyo.quote: Nobody told me that the hardest part of living in Tokyo isn't the language — it's figuring out which convenience store is your convenience store. Once you have that, you have a home.

marcus-kyoto.quote: I moved to Kyoto for a research program and stayed for the mornings. At 6am, before the tour groups arrive, this city belongs to you in a way that feels almost unfair.

priya-osaka.quote: Osaka is the first place outside India where strangers talked to me in line at a restaurant. Not tourist-talk. Real talk. About food, about the neighborhood, about where I was from. I didn't expect that.

james-tokyo.quote: The loneliness hit in year two. Year one is euphoria, year two is reality. What helped was finding Shimokitazawa — that neighborhood saved me. It felt like a place that made room for odd people.

elena-kyoto.quote: I failed the JLPT N4 twice before I realized I was studying for a test, not for a life. The day I stopped studying and just started talking to my neighbor, everything changed.

david-osaka.quote: Finding my apartment in Osaka took four months and three rejections because I was foreign. When I finally got the place in Namba, the landlord apologized and took me out for kushikatsu. Japan will break your heart and then feed you.

about.title: About MA
about.quote: Not a travel guide. A feeling, honestly shared.
about.choose_mood: Each one feels different. Choose the mood you are in.
about.manifesto_1: Most writing about Japan is wrong — not factually, but emotionally. It reduces a civilization of extraordinary depth to a list of things to do and places to see. It treats mystery as a problem to be solved, silence as an absence to be filled.
about.manifesto_2: MA began from a different premise: that Japan deserves to be written about the way it actually feels. Electric and lonely in Tokyo at 3am. Quiet and ancient in Kyoto before the crowds. Warm and unguarded in Osaka over a bowl of ramen that someone has been perfecting for thirty years.
about.manifesto_3: We are not a travel guide. We do not tell you what to do. We tell you what it feels like to be there — the specific texture of certain hours in certain places, the emotional weather of cities that have been shaped by centuries of particular values: restraint, precision, beauty, impermanence.
about.manifesto_4: The name comes from 間 (ma), a Japanese concept with no direct English translation. It means the space between things — the pause between notes that makes music meaningful, the gap between objects that gives them definition, the silence that makes speech worth hearing. Every piece we publish lives in that space.
about.manifesto_5: We write slowly, carefully, and honestly. We do not publish AI-generated content. We do not optimize for search engines. We do not produce lists. We produce felt experiences, honestly recalled.
about.manifesto_6: Japan is not a destination. It is a feeling. We are trying to share it.
about.value_honest_desc: We write from real experience. No press trips, no sponsored content, no AI-generated text. Every word is accountable to the actual feeling of being somewhere.
about.value_slow_desc: We publish rarely and carefully. One well-observed moment is worth more than a hundred rushed dispatches.
about.value_literary_desc: We treat travel writing as literature — with all the craft, ambiguity, and emotional honesty that implies.
about.value_specific_desc: We resist generalization. The feeling of Tokyo at 3am in November rain is different from Tokyo at noon in August. We care about the difference.

shimokitazawa.description: Vintage clothes, live music, tiny theatre, and the sense that it's 1992 in the best possible way. Where Tokyo's artists, students, and quiet rebels have always lived.
shimokitazawa.insiderTip: The Sunday flea market behind Honda Theater starts at 9am. Go early — the good stuff is gone by 10.

yanaka.description: A neighborhood that survived the war and the real estate developers both. Cemetery walks, shotengai shopping streets, cats on every corner. The Tokyo that Tokyo forgot to modernize.
yanaka.insiderTip: Yanaka Ginza at dusk, when the shops are closing and the smell of yakitori fills the narrow street, is worth any detour.

gion.description: Yes, the tourists come. But at 6am and 10pm, Gion belongs to the people who live in it. Cobbled lanes, wooden machiya houses, the sound of wooden sandals. It earns its reputation.
gion.insiderTip: Hanamikoji-dori at 7am on a weekday. You might be the only person on the street. Bring a camera. Don't use it.

namba.description: The beating heart of Osaka. Overwhelming at first, then familiar, then something close to home. Street food, arcade sounds, the mechanical crab, and somehow underneath all of it, a genuine warmth.
namba.insiderTip: The ramen shops in the alleys east of Dotonbori — away from the canal — have lower prices and no queues. Locals eat there. Tourists eat near the water.

tip-1.tip: Your local konbini is your second home. Learn the staff's faces. Smile. They remember.

tip-2.tip: Japan runs on cash. Keep ¥10,000 on you at all times. Not every restaurant takes cards, and the moment you're caught without cash will be embarrassing.

tip-3.tip: Live north of Oike-dori and east of Kawaramachi-dori. Tourist Kyoto is south. Real Kyoto is everywhere else.

tip-4.tip: The most useful Japanese phrase is not 'sumimasen'. It's knowing when to bow and when to be silent. Language is 30% words.

tip-5.tip: Osaka locals eat standing up and fast. If a ramen shop has no chairs, that's a good sign, not a bad one.

tip-6.tip: Get a guarantor service if you don't have a Japanese guarantor. They cost money (usually one month's rent) but open 80% of apartments that would otherwise reject foreign applicants.
tip-6.context: Community advice — confirmed by multiple members

today.title: Tokyo prepared something small for you today.
today.map_bridge: While you're out, the city has memories attached to places. Walk through any of these neighborhoods and you'll find fragments of other people's Tokyo — collected over time, unlocked on foot.

yoyogi-sunday.title: Yoyogi Park Sundays
yoyogi-sunday.hook: Every Sunday, the park becomes a hundred different lives you can walk through.
yoyogi-sunday.body:
In Yoyogi Park on a Sunday afternoon, the city stops performing. Bands practice in the shade of old trees. Strangers throw frisbees. A man in his seventies plays guitar badly and doesn't care who hears. Dogs sleep in patches of sunlight.

You don't need Japanese. You don't need a plan. You can sit on the grass for an hour and leave with a feeling you weren't expecting — that Tokyo is not as lonely as your room makes it seem.

Enter from the Harajuku gate. Arrive sometime after noon and stay until you feel ready to leave.

shimokitazawa-sunday-task.title: Shimokitazawa Before the Crowd
shimokitazawa-sunday-task.hook: The vintage shops are open. The owners are drinking coffee and not watching you.
shimokitazawa-sunday-task.body:
Arrive before noon on a Sunday. The south side is technically open but feels private. The shop owners are playing records they chose themselves. The streets smell like cedar and old cotton.

You're not expected to buy anything. Browse slowly. Try on something you'd never normally wear and put it back. This is practice for living in a city — learning how to be present in a place without needing to extract something from it.

sensoji-monday.title: Sensoji Before 9am
sensoji-monday.hook: The most visited temple in Japan — in the thirty minutes before it belongs to anyone else.
sensoji-monday.body:
At 7am, Sensoji is a different building entirely. The vendors are still setting up. The incense hasn't had to compete with anything yet. An elderly woman moves through the grounds without hurrying, not photographing anything.

There are perhaps forty people here when there will soon be forty thousand. The wooden structure sounds different in early morning air — quiet, present, slightly unreal.

Take the Ginza Line to Asakusa. Buy a hot canned coffee from the machine just before the gate. Arrive with no agenda. Leave before the tour groups find it.

nakameguro-monday-task.title: Nakameguro Canal After Dark
nakameguro-monday-task.hook: The canal at night is quieter than the photos make it look.
nakameguro-monday-task.body:
Weekday evenings, the canal path belongs to couples walking slowly and people who have finished work and are not ready to go home yet. The water reflects the restaurant lights. Cats appear and disappear between buildings.

Walk the full length one direction. Pick somewhere for a drink on the way back — anywhere with seats facing the water. You'll be there longer than you planned. That's the correct outcome.

top-museum-tuesday.title: Tokyo Photographic Art Museum
top-museum-tuesday.hook: Four floors of photography, and almost nobody in your program knows this place exists.
top-museum-tuesday.body:
TOP runs three or four exhibitions simultaneously, rotating regularly through Japanese and international photographers. The building is quiet in a way Tokyo almost never is — the specific silence of spaces that take images seriously.

Tuesday is usually the least crowded weekday. The museum is in Yebisu Garden Place, a former Sapporo brewery complex with a good plaza outside. Come for the exhibition. Stay for the plaza.

¥500–900. Yebisu station, 8 minutes walk.

kuramae-tuesday-task.title: Kuramae: The Craft District
kuramae-tuesday-task.hook: The neighborhood where people make things with their hands and sell them out the front.
kuramae-tuesday-task.body:
Kuramae has become Tokyo's small craft and design district — independent workshops, stationers, leather workers, pottery studios that also function as shops. Tuesday is quiet and unhurried.

Walk from Kuramae station toward the river. There is no itinerary. The point is to notice what catches your attention and follow it. There's a particular satisfaction in owning something handmade in a city that usually moves fast.

language-exchange-wednesday.title: Language Exchange, Wednesday Evening
language-exchange-wednesday.hook: An hour of Japanese practice with someone who wants your English just as much.
language-exchange-wednesday.body:
The format removes most of the anxiety: twenty minutes of Japanese, twenty minutes of English, switching back and forth until it feels like a conversation.

Most participants are in their twenties — students and workers. The goal is not fluency. It's contact, the specific kind you don't get from apps. The chance to speak to someone in Tokyo who is just as uncertain about something as you are.

Free plus the price of a drink. Wednesday evenings from 18:30.

yanaka-wednesday-task.title: Yanaka at Dusk
yanaka-wednesday-task.hook: The neighborhood that survived both the earthquake and the developers.
yanaka-wednesday-task.body:
Yanaka is one of the few parts of Tokyo where the streets haven't been rebuilt since the Showa period. The houses are wooden. The alleys don't follow a grid. The cemetery at the center of the neighborhood is enormous and very calm at dusk — locals walk through it on the way home.

Arriving around 17:00 gives you two hours before dark. Walk slowly. The cats here are famous. The view from Yanaka Ginza toward the sunset is unspectacular in a way that is somehow perfect.

koenji-jazz-thursday.title: Kōenji: The Jazz Bars
koenji-jazz-thursday.hook: You don't have to know anything about jazz to sit in one of these and feel like you do.
koenji-jazz-thursday.body:
North of Koenji station, behind the shotengai, there are four or five small jazz bars that seem to exist slightly outside of regular time. The same record collection since 1974. The same bar stools. The bartenders are serious about the music without being unfriendly about it.

Showing up alone is normal and possibly preferred. Order a whisky or whatever they have cold. Stay for one full album before you decide whether to leave.

¥500–1,500 entry plus drinks. Thursday through Saturday from 20:00.

arakawa-thursday-task.title: Arakawa River at Dusk
arakawa-thursday-task.hook: A wide sky and a long path, where nobody is going anywhere important.
arakawa-thursday-task.body:
The Arakawa embankment path runs through a part of Tokyo that most visitors never reach — genuinely residential, working-class, without atmosphere management of any kind.

Evening walks here have a specific quality: the sky is huge, the air smells like a river rather than concrete, and the people you pass are locals exercising or doing nothing in particular. No recommendations to look up, no photographs anyone has taken before.

From Nishi-Arakawa station. Walk north along the embankment. Turn around when you feel like it.

shimokitazawa-music-friday.title: Live Music in Shimokitazawa
shimokitazawa-music-friday.hook: Small venues where you can see the guitarist's hands from your seat.
shimokitazawa-music-friday.body:
Friday evenings, the live music venues in Shimokitazawa's south side all have shows. The format is almost always the same: a hundred-person maximum, drink ticket included, bands playing whatever they play — indie, folk, experimental, occasionally very loud.

You don't need to research who's playing. Pick a venue with a show starting at 19:30 or 20:00 and go. The experience of being in a small room with music happening matters more than the specific band.

¥1,500–3,000 including one drink. Shimokitazawa south exit.

golden-gai-friday-task.title: Shinjuku Golden Gai
golden-gai-friday-task.hook: Two hundred bars. Sit in one. See what happens.
golden-gai-friday-task.body:
Six narrow lanes packed with bars that hold eight to twelve people maximum. Each has its own logic — film posters, avant-garde jazz, a bartender who speaks five languages, or one who barely speaks at all.

The ones with menus outside or a small English sign are happy to have newcomers. Order whatever they're pouring. The correct number of bars to visit in one evening is two or three. Arrive at 21:00. Leave when it feels right.

koenji-market-saturday.title: Kōenji Morning Market
koenji-market-saturday.hook: Old things at honest prices, before anyone announces it on Instagram.
koenji-market-saturday.body:
Every weekend outside Koenji station, a flea market spreads across the plaza with vendors selling records, old clothes, ceramics, and objects with no obvious purpose. The vendors are not curating a brand — they are selling things they own that other people might want.

The best finds are gone by noon. Go at 9 or 10, while people are still setting up. Cash only. No English required — pointing works perfectly. The light in Koenji on a Saturday morning is very good.

South exit of Koenji station. Free entry.

nishi-ogikubo-saturday-task.title: Nishi-Ogikubo Antiques
nishi-ogikubo-saturday-task.hook: The antique district most tourists have never heard of, three stops west of Shinjuku.
nishi-ogikubo-saturday-task.body:
A cluster of antique and used furniture shops that Tokyo designers have known about for decades. Showa-era appliances, mid-century lamps, kimono fabric, objects that are neither vintage-trendy nor historically significant but interesting in ways that resist explanation.

Looking is free. The walk from the station takes you through a genuinely residential neighborhood that feels nothing like central Tokyo. Plan two hours, bring cash if you want to buy anything, and bring nothing in particular. The goal is to notice things.

tokyo.description: Tokyo does not sleep. It hums — a low, constant frequency beneath forty million heartbeats. Here, loneliness is not an absence but a texture: the feel of 3am convenience store light on wet pavement, the weight of a crowd that moves around you like water. Electric, anonymous, and somehow more alive than anywhere else on earth.
tokyo.feelings: Electric anonymity|3am vending machines|The loneliness of crowds|Neon in the rain

kyoto.description: Kyoto does not rush. It waits — in the moss between old stones, in the pause before a temple bell, in the way morning light crosses a paper screen. This is a city that remembers everything: the weight of silk, the smell of cedar and incense, the sound of wooden sandals on a cobbled lane at dusk. It makes you nostalgic for a life you have never lived.
kyoto.feelings: Ancient silence|Moss and cedar|The weight of centuries|Morning temple bells

osaka.description: Osaka does not hold back. It feeds you, it teases you, it pulls you into a conversation you did not know you were having. This is Japan without the formality — where strangers share tables, where food is religion, where the city laughs at itself. Dotonbori at midnight is the most human place in the world: chaotic, warm, and completely honest about what it wants.
osaka.feelings: Street food warmth|Dotonbori midnight|Laughter without reason|The democracy of hunger
